search_method: The search was structured directly from the branch/comparison surface of merge.py as written. The code has exactly three decision points: (1) the emptiness test on line 3, (2) the lexicographic sort on line 5 (whose only behavioral wrinkle is tie-breaking on equal starts), and (3) the strict comparison `s < out[-1][1]` on line 8, together with the `max(out[-1][1], e)` on line 9 inside its true branch. For each comparison I enumerated both sides plus the equality boundary: empty vs non-empty; sort with distinct starts, equal starts, and identical intervals; line 8 with s < end (overlap), s > end (disjoint), and the boundary s == end (touching); line 9 with e > end (extends) and e <= end (nested). Each class got at least one concrete in-domain candidate that was hand-simulated line by line, and every output was sorted and checked pairwise against the predicate i.end >= j.start. Independently of the class analysis, a bounded structural family of two-interval cases [a,b],[c,d] over endpoints in {-1,0,1,2} was enumerated by the exhaustive case split on the relation of c to b (disjoint / touching / overlapping / nested / identical / zero-width variants), with representatives of each relation simulated concretely. Both the class-driven search and the structural sweep converge on the same fault: the strict '<' on line 8 means an interval whose start equals the current merged end is appended rather than merged, and any such appended pair (prev_end == next_start) satisfies i.end >= j.start in the sorted output. The first mechanical violation encountered was [[0,1],[1,2]]; the search continued through all planned classes and found the same boundary fault in every touching-class candidate, and no violation in any non-touching class.
